Jefferson was born on April 13, 1743 (April 2, 1743, [Old Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style "Old Style"), [Julian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_calendar "Julian calendar")), at the family's [Shadwell Plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadwell,_Virginia "Shadwell, Virginia") in the [Colony of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia "Colony of Virginia"). He was the third of ten children.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-7) His father, [Peter Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Jefferson "Peter Jefferson"), was a planter and surveyor; his mother was [Jane Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Randolph_Jefferson "Jane Randolph Jefferson").[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-10) Peter Jefferson moved his family to [Tuckahoe Plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuckahoe_Plantation "Tuckahoe Plantation") in 1745 following the death of [William Randolph III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Randolph_III_(son_of_Thomas) "William Randolph III (son of Thomas)"), the plantation's owner and Jefferson's friend, who in his will had named Peter guardian of Randolph's children. The Jeffersons returned to Shadwell before October 1753.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-11)

Jefferson began his education together with the [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_family_of_Virginia "Randolph family of Virginia") children at Tuckahoe under tutors.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-12) Thomas' father Peter, who was self-taught and regretted not having a formal education, entered Thomas into an English school at age five. In 1752, at age nine, he attended a local school run by a [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian") minister and also began studying the natural world, which he grew to love. He studied [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin"), [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"), and [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"), and began learning to ride horses. Thomas read books from his father's modest library.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-bowers12-13) He was taught from 1758 to 1760 by the Reverend [James Maury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Maury "James Maury") near [Gordonsville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordonsville,_Virginia "Gordonsville, Virginia"), where he studied history, science, and the [classics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classics "Classics") while boarding with Maury's family.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-bowers12-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-14) Jefferson came to know various Native Americans including [Cherokee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherokee "Cherokee") chief [Ostenaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostenaco "Ostenaco"), who often stopped at Shadwell to visit on their way to [Williamsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williamsburg,_Virginia "Williamsburg, Virginia") to trade.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-15)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-16) In Williamsburg, the young Jefferson met and came to admire [Patrick Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Henry "Patrick Henry").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-17)

Thomas's father died in 1757, and his estate was divided between his sons, Thomas and [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Jefferson "Randolph Jefferson").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-18)[John Harvie Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harvie_Sr. "John Harvie Sr.") became 14-year-old Thomas' guardian.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Woods-19) Thomas inherited approximately 5,000 acres (7.8 sq mi; 20.2 km 2), which included the land on which he later built [Monticello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monticello "Monticello") in 1772.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Malone437-20)

In 1761, at the age of seventeen, Jefferson entered the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary") in Williamsburg, where he studied mathematics and philosophy with [William Small](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Small "William Small"). Under Small's tutelage, Jefferson encountered the ideas of British [empiricists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empiricists "Empiricists"), including [John Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke "John Locke"), [Francis Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Bacon "Francis Bacon"), and [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton"). Small also introduced Jefferson to [George Wythe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wythe "George Wythe") and [Francis Fauquier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Fauquier "Francis Fauquier"). Small, Wythe, and Fauquier recognized Jefferson as a man of exceptional ability and included him in their inner circle, where he became a regular member of their Friday dinner parties. Jefferson later wrote that, while there, he "heard more common good sense, more rational & philosophical conversations than in all the rest of my life".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-21)

During his first year in college, Jefferson spent considerable time attending parties and dancing and was not very frugal with his expenditures; in his second year, regretting that he had squandered away time and money in his first year, he committed to studying fifteen hours a day.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-22) While at William & Mary, Jefferson became a member of the [Flat Hat Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_Hat_Club "Flat Hat Club"), the nation's oldest secret society, a small group whose members included St. George Tucker, Edmund Randolph, and James Innes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-24)

Jefferson concluded his formal studies in April 1762.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-25) He [read the law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read_the_law "Read the law") under Wythe's tutelage while working as a [law clerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk") in his office.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-26) Jefferson was well-read in a broad variety of subjects, including law, philosophy, history, natural law, natural religion, ethics,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and several areas of science, including astronomy[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-27) and agriculture.

Jefferson kept two [commonplace books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonplace_book "Commonplace book"): from about age 15 to 30, he compiled a book of sayings and quotations, published in the 20th century as _Jefferson's Literary Commonplace Book_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-28) During his years of legal study under Wythe, Jefferson began recording his notes on law, history, and philosophy, and continued to do so until the end of his life; his _Legal Commonplace Book_ was also published in the 20th century.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-29)

On July 20, 1765, Jefferson's sister Martha married his close friend and college companion [Dabney Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dabney_Carr_(Virginia_assemblyman) "Dabney Carr (Virginia assemblyman)"), which greatly pleased Jefferson. In October of that year, however, Jefferson's sister Jane unexpectedly died at age 25. Her death plunged Jefferson into a months-long period of mourning that was spoken of amongst the family.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-30)

Jefferson treasured his books and amassed three sizable libraries in his lifetime. He began assembling his first library, which grew to 200 volumes, in his youth.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-31) Wythe was so impressed with Jefferson that he later bequeathed his entire library to him.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-32) In 1770, however, Jefferson's first library was destroyed in a fire at his Shadwell home. His second library, which replenished the first, grew to nearly 6,500 volumes by 1814.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-33) After [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland") forces set the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") on fire in the [Burning of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_of_Washington "Burning of Washington") in 1814, Jefferson sold his second library to the [U.S. government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._government "U.S. government") for $23,950, hoping to help jumpstart the Library of Congress's rebuilding. Jefferson used a portion of the proceeds to pay off some of his large debt. Jefferson soon resumed collecting his third personal library. In a letter to John Adams, Jefferson wrote, "I cannot live without books."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-library-34)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-35) By the time of Jefferson's death a decade later, his third and final library had grown to nearly 2,000 volumes.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-36)

## Career

Main article: [Early life and career of Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_life_and_career_of_Thomas_Jefferson "Early life and career of Thomas Jefferson")

### Lawyer and House of Burgesses

Further information: [A Summary View of the Rights of British America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Summary_View_of_the_Rights_of_British_America "A Summary View of the Rights of British America")

In 1767, Jefferson was granted admission to the Virginia bar, and lived with his mother at Shadwell.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-37) Between 1769 and 1775, he represented [Albemarle County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albemarle_County "Albemarle County") in Virginia's [House of Burgesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Burgesses "House of Burgesses").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-38) While serving in the House of Burgesses, Jefferson pursued reforms to slavery, including writing and sponsoring legislation in 1769 to strip power from the royal governor and courts, instead providing masters of slaves with the discretion to emancipate them. Jefferson persuaded his cousin [Richard Bland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bland "Richard Bland") to spearhead the legislation's passage, but it faced strong opposition in a state whose economy was largely agrarian.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-39)

As a lawyer, Jefferson took on seven freedom-seeking enslaved people as clients[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-40) and [waived his fee for one](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_bono "Pro bono") he claimed should be freed before the minimum statutory age for emancipation.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Gordon99-41) Jefferson invoked [natural law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_law "Natural law"), arguing "everyone comes into the world with a right to his own person and using it at his own will... This is what is called personal liberty, and is given him by the author of nature, because it is necessary for his own sustenance." The judge cut him off and ruled against his client. As a consolation, Jefferson gave his client some money, which was conceivably used to aid his escape shortly thereafter.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Gordon99-41) Jefferson's underlying intellectual argument that all people were entitled by their creator to what he labeled a "natural right" to liberty is a theme that he later prominently incorporated into the Declaration of Independence.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-42) In 1767, Jefferson took on 68 cases for the General Court of Virginia and was counsel in three notable cases of that era, _Howell v. Netherland_ (1770), _Bolling v. Bolling_ (1771), and _Blair v. Blair_ (1772).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Konig_Time_Line-43)

In 1774, Jefferson authored a resolution calling for a boycott of all British goods in protest of the [British Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Great_Britain "Parliament of Great Britain")'s passing of the [Intolerable Acts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intolerable_Acts "Intolerable Acts"). Jefferson's resolution was later expanded into _[A Summary View of the Rights of British America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Summary\_View\_of\_the\_Rights\_of\_British\_America "A Summary View of the Rights of British America")_, published that year in which he argued that people have the right to [govern themselves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governing_colony "Self-governing colony").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-44)

## Monticello, marriage, and family

Further information: [Martha Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Jefferson "Martha Jefferson") and [Monticello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monticello "Monticello")

[![Image 11: Monticello plantation house](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Monticello_2010-10-29.jpg/250px-Monticello_2010-10-29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monticello_2010-10-29.jpg)

[Monticello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monticello "Monticello"), Jefferson's home near [Charlottesville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottesville,_Virginia "Charlottesville, Virginia")

In 1768, Jefferson began constructing his primary residence, [Monticello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monticello "Monticello"), on a hilltop overlooking his 5,000-acre (20 km 2; 7.8 mi 2) plantation.[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-46) He spent most of his adult life designing Monticello and was quoted as saying, "Architecture is my delight, and putting up, and pulling down, one of my favorite amusements."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-47) Construction was done mostly by local masons and carpenters, assisted by Jefferson's slaves.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-48) He moved into the South Pavilion in 1770. Turning Monticello into a [neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") masterpiece in the [Palladian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palladian "Palladian") style became Jefferson's lifelong project.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-49)

On January 1, 1772, Jefferson married his third cousin,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-50)[Martha Wayles Skelton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Wayles_Skelton "Martha Wayles Skelton"), a 23-year-old widow of Bathurst Skelton.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Tucker_p.47-51)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-52) She was a frequent hostess for Jefferson and managed the large household. Historian [Dumas Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dumas_Malone "Dumas Malone") described the marriage as the happiest period of Jefferson's life.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-53) Martha was a skilled pianist; Jefferson often accompanied her on the violin or cello.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-54) During their ten-year marriage, Martha bore six children: [Martha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Jefferson_Randolph "Martha Jefferson Randolph") "Patsy" (1772–1836); Jane Randolph (1774–1775); an unnamed son who lived for only a few weeks in 1777; [Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Jefferson_Eppes "Mary Jefferson Eppes") "Polly" (1778–1804); Lucy Elizabeth (1780–1781); and another Lucy Elizabeth (1782–1784).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-55)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-58) Only Martha and Mary survived to adulthood.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Martha-59) Martha's father, John Wayles, died in 1773, and the couple inherited 135 enslaved people, 11,000 acres (45 km 2; 17 mi 2), and the estate's debts. The debts took Jefferson years to satisfy, contributing to his financial problems.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Tucker_p.47-51)

Martha later suffered from ill health, including [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes "Diabetes"), and frequent childbirth weakened her. A few months after the birth of her last child, she died on September 6, 1782, with Jefferson at her bedside. Shortly before her death, Martha made Jefferson promise never to marry again, telling him that she could not bear to have another mother raise her children.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-60) Jefferson was grief-stricken by her death, relentlessly pacing back and forth for roughly three weeks, and finally emerging to take long rambling rides on secluded roads with his daughter, Martha, who said she was "a solitary witness to many a violent burst of grief".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Martha-59)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Halliday48-61)

## Revolutionary War

### Declaration of Independence

Main article: [United States Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence "United States Declaration of Independence")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence.jpg/250px-United_States_Declaration_of_Independence.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:United_States_Declaration_of_Independence.jpg)

The [Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence "United States Declaration of Independence"), which Jefferson largely wrote in isolation between June 11 and 28, 1776, from a floor he was renting in a home at 700 [Market Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_Street_(Philadelphia) "Market Street (Philadelphia)") in [Center City Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_City_Philadelphia "Center City Philadelphia"),[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-nps.gov-62) contain "the most potent and consequential words in American history," historian [Joseph Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Ellis "Joseph Ellis") later wrote.

Jefferson was the primary author of the [Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence "United States Declaration of Independence").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-63) At age 33, he was one of the youngest delegates to the [Second Continental Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Continental_Congress "Second Continental Congress"), which convened in the colonial capital of [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") following the [Battles of Lexington and Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battles_of_Lexington_and_Concord "Battles of Lexington and Concord"), which launched the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War") in 1775. Delegates to the Congress overwhelmingly favored authoring, ratifying, and issuing a formal declaration of independence from Britain.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-64) Jefferson was inspired by the [Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment "Age of Enlightenment") ideals of the sanctity of the individual, and the writings of [Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke "John Locke") and [Montesquieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montesquieu "Montesquieu").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-65)

Jefferson sought out John Adams, a Continental Congress delegate from [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Massachusetts_Bay "Province of Massachusetts Bay") and an emerging leader in the Congress.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-66) They became close friends, and Adams supported Jefferson's appointment to the [Committee of Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_of_Five "Committee of Five"), which the Congress charged with authoring the Declaration: Adams, Jefferson, [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin "Benjamin Franklin"), [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), and [Roger Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Sherman "Roger Sherman"). The committee initially thought that Adams should write the document, but Adams persuaded the committee to choose Jefferson due to Jefferson being a Virginian, popular, and a good writer by Adams.[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-68)

Jefferson consulted with his fellow committee members, but mostly wrote the Declaration of Independence in isolation between June 11 and 28, 1776.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-nps.gov-62) Jefferson drew considerably on his proposed draft of the [Virginia Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Constitution "Virginia Constitution"), [George Mason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mason "George Mason")'s draft of the [Virginia Declaration of Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Declaration_of_Rights "Virginia Declaration of Rights"), and other sources.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-69) Other committee members made some changes, and a final draft was presented to Congress on June 28, 1776.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Meacham,_2012,_p._105-70) Congress began debate over its contents on Monday, July 1,[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Meacham,_2012,_p._105-70) resulting in the removal of roughly a fourth of Jefferson's original draft.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-71)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Ellis,_1996,_p._50-72) Jefferson resented the changes, but he did not speak publicly about them.[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-74) On July 4, 1776, the Congress voted unanimously to ratify the Declaration, and delegates signed it on August 2. Jefferson and the other delegates knew they were committing [high treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_treason_in_the_United_Kingdom "High treason in the United Kingdom") against [the Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crown "The Crown"), which was punishable by [torture and death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanged,_drawn_and_quartered "Hanged, drawn and quartered").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-75)

Following its ratification, the Declaration was released publicly. Two days after its ratification, on July 6, _[The Pennsylvania Evening Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pennsylvania\_Evening\_Post "The Pennsylvania Evening Post")_, was the first newspaper to publish it. On July 8 at noon, it was read publicly and simultaneously for the first time at three designated locations: [Trenton, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trenton,_New_Jersey "Trenton, New Jersey"); [Easton, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton,_Pennsylvania "Easton, Pennsylvania"); and Philadelphia.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-76)

Contemporary historians generally view the Declaration of Independence as one of the most significant and influential written documents in world history, and Jefferson's preamble is regarded as an enduring statement on [individual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual_and_group_rights "Individual and group rights") and [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights"). Jefferson's phrase "[all men are created equal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_men_are_created_equal "All men are created equal")" has been called "one of the best-known sentences in the English language". [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") history chairman [David Armitage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Armitage_(historian) "David Armitage (historian)") has written that, "No American document has had a greater global impact than the Declaration of Independence",[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-77) and historian [Joseph Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Ellis "Joseph Ellis") has written that the Declaration includes "the most potent and consequential words in American history".[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Ellis,_1996,_p._50-72)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-78)

### Virginia state legislator and governor

[![Image 13: Governor's Palace](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/The_Governor%27s_Palace_--_Williamsburg_%28VA%29_September_2012.jpg/250px-The_Governor%27s_Palace_--_Williamsburg_%28VA%29_September_2012.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Governor's_Palace_--_Williamsburg_(VA)_September_2012.jpg)

[Governor's Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor's_Palace_(Williamsburg,_Virginia) "Governor's Palace (Williamsburg, Virginia)"), Jefferson's residence in [Williamsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williamsburg,_Virginia "Williamsburg, Virginia") during his term as Virginia's governor from 1779 to 1781

At the start of the American Revolution, [Colonel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_(United_States) "Colonel (United States)") Jefferson was named commander of the [Albemarle County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albemarle_County "Albemarle County") Militia on September 26, 1775.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-79) He was then elected to the [Virginia House of Delegates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_House_of_Delegates "Virginia House of Delegates") for Albemarle County in September 1776, when finalizing the state constitution was a priority.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Peterson_pp._101-80)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Fer26-81) For nearly three years, Jefferson assisted with the constitution and was especially proud of his Bill for Establishing Religious Freedom, which prohibited state support of religious institutions or enforcement of religious doctrine.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-82) The bill failed to pass, as did his legislation to disestablish the [Anglican Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church "Anglican Church"), but both were later revived by [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-83)

In 1778, Jefferson was given the task of revising the state's laws. He drafted 126 bills in three years, including laws to streamline the judicial system. He proposed statutes that provided for general education, which he considered the basis of "republican government".[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Peterson_pp._101-80) Jefferson also was concerned that Virginia's powerful landed gentry were becoming a hereditary aristocracy and took the lead in abolishing what he called "feudal and unnatural distinctions".[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Brewer-84) He targeted laws such as [entail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entail "Entail") and [primogeniture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primogeniture "Primogeniture") by which a deceased landowner's oldest son was vested with all land ownership and power.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Brewer-84)[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-86)

Jefferson was elected [governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Virginia "Governor of Virginia") for one-year terms in 1779 and 1780.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-87) He transferred the state capital from Williamsburg to [Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia"), and introduced additional measures for public education, religious freedom, and inheritance.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-88)

During General [Benedict Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_Arnold "Benedict Arnold")'s 1781 [invasion of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raid_on_Richmond "Raid on Richmond"), Jefferson escaped Richmond just ahead of the British forces, which razed the city.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-89)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-90) He sent emergency dispatches to Colonel [Sampson Mathews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampson_Mathews "Sampson Mathews") and other commanders in an attempt to repel Arnold's efforts.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-91)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-92) When the British occupied [Norfolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk,_Virginia "Norfolk, Virginia"), Jefferson had caused patriots to burn and destroy it in 1776.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-93)[General Charles Cornwallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Charles_Cornwallis "General Charles Cornwallis") that spring dispatched a cavalry force led by [Banastre Tarleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banastre_Tarleton "Banastre Tarleton") to capture Jefferson and members of the Assembly at Monticello, but [Jack Jouett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Jouett "Jack Jouett") of the [Virginia militia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_militia "Virginia militia") thwarted the British plan.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-96) Jefferson escaped to [Poplar Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poplar_Forest "Poplar Forest"), his plantation to the west.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-97) When the General Assembly reconvened in June 1781, it conducted an inquiry into Jefferson's actions which eventually concluded that Jefferson had acted with honor, but Jefferson was not reelected.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-98)

In April of the same year, his daughter Lucy died at age one. A second daughter of that name was born the following year, but she died at age two.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-99)

In 1782, Jefferson refused a partnership offer by North Carolina Governor [Abner Nash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abner_Nash "Abner Nash"), in a profiteering scheme involving the sale of confiscated Loyalist lands.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-100) Unlike some Founders, Jefferson was content with his Monticello estate and the land he owned in the vicinity of Virginia's [Shenandoah Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenandoah_Valley "Shenandoah Valley"). Jefferson thought of Monticello as an intellectual gathering place for [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison"), [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe "James Monroe"), and other friends.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-101)

Jefferson accused British-based merchants of unfairly depressing tobacco prices and forcing Virginia planters to take on unsustainable debt loads. In 1786, he remarked:

> A powerful engine for this [mercantile profiteering] was the giving of good prices and credit to the planter till they got him more immersed in debt than he could pay without selling lands or slaves. They then reduced the prices given for his tobacco so that…they never permitted him to clear off his debt.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-102)

### _Notes on the State of Virginia_

Main article: [Notes on the State of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notes_on_the_State_of_Virginia "Notes on the State of Virginia")

In 1780, Jefferson received a letter of inquiry from French diplomat [François Barbé-Marbois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Barb%C3%A9-Marbois "François Barbé-Marbois") into the geography, history, and government of Virginia, as part of a study of the United States. Jefferson organized his responses in a book, _Notes on the State of Virginia_ (1785).[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-103) The book explores what constitutes a good society, using Virginia as an exemplar. Jefferson included extensive data about the state's natural resources and economy and wrote at length about slavery and [miscegenation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscegenation "Miscegenation"); he articulated his belief that blacks and whites could not live together as free people in one society because of justified resentments of the enslaved.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-104) He also wrote of his views on the American Indians, equating them to European settlers.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-105)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-106)

_Notes_ was first published in 1785 in [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_(language) "French (language)") and appeared in English in 1787.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-107) Biographer [George Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Tucker_(author) "George Tucker (author)") considered the work "surprising in the extent of the information which a single individual had been thus far able to acquire, as to the physical features of the state";[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-108)[University of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Virginia "University of Virginia") historian [Merrill D. Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_D._Peterson "Merrill D. Peterson") described it as an accomplishment for which all Americans should be grateful.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-109)

## Member of Congress

Further information: [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation")

[![Image 14: Legislative chamber](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Independence_Hall_Assembly_Room.jpg/250px-Independence_Hall_Assembly_Room.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Independence_Hall_Assembly_Room.jpg)

The Assembly Room at [Independence Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Hall "Independence Hall") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), where Jefferson served as a delegate to the [Second Continental Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Continental_Congress "Second Continental Congress") and where the Congress edited but unanimously ratified his draft of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776

Jefferson was appointed a Virginia delegate to the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") organized following the [peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1783) "Treaty of Paris (1783)") with Great Britain in 1783. He was a member of the committee setting foreign exchange rates and [recommended](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan_for_Establishing_Uniformity_in_the_Coinage,_Weights,_and_Measures_of_the_United_States "Plan for Establishing Uniformity in the Coinage, Weights, and Measures of the United States") an American currency based on the decimal system that was adopted.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-110) He advised the formation of the [Committee of the States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_of_the_States "Committee of the States") to fill the power vacuum when Congress was in recess.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-111) The committee met when Congress adjourned, but disagreements rendered it dysfunctional.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-112)

Jefferson sent a letter (revealed in 2025) to Virginia Governor [Benjamin Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Harrison_V "Benjamin Harrison V"), dated December 31, 1783, in which he relates the wave of enthusiasm of Europeans for taking up arms against their leaders. Jefferson was sharing the affirmation of his own promotion of the right to bear arms that brought about the American Revolution. The letter also conveys Jefferson's anxiety over the final ratification of the Treaty of Paris formally ending the revolutionary war. Signed initially by the parties in September, the still-outstanding consent of two colonies was required in London (then a two-month journey) by the following March. The deadline was ultimately but barely met, with the required signatures made in mid-January.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-113)

In the Congress's 1783–1784 session, Jefferson acted as chairman of committees to establish a viable system of government for the new Republic and to propose a policy for settlement of the western territories. He was the principal author of the [Land Ordinance of 1784](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Ordinance_of_1784 "Land Ordinance of 1784"), whereby Virginia ceded to the national government the vast area that it claimed northwest of the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River"). He insisted that this territory should not be used as colonial territory by any of the thirteen states, but that it should be divided into sections that could become states. He plotted borders for nine new states in their initial stages and wrote an ordinance banning slavery in all the nation's territories. Congress made extensive revisions and rejected the ban on slavery.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Peretson189-114)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-115) The provisions banning slavery, known as the "Jefferson Proviso", were modified and implemented three years later in the [Northwest Ordinance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Ordinance "Northwest Ordinance") of 1787 and became the law for the entire [Northwest Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Territory "Northwest Territory").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Peretson189-114)

## Minister to France

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Grille_De_Chaillot.jpg/250px-Grille_De_Chaillot.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grille_De_Chaillot.jpg)

A 1779 engraving of [Champs-Élysées](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Champs-%C3%89lys%C3%A9es "Champs-Élysées") seen through the Grille de Chaillot with Jefferson's residence in Paris on the left

On May 7, 1784, Jefferson was appointed by the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation")[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-116) to join [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin "Benjamin Franklin") and John Adams in Paris as Minister [Plenipotentiary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plenipotentiary "Plenipotentiary") for Negotiating Treaties of Amity and Commerce with [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") and other countries.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-117)[[j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-119) With his young daughter Patsy and two servants, he departed in July 1784, arriving in Paris the next month.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Stewart39-120)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-121) Jefferson had Patsy educated at [Pentemont Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentemont_Abbey "Pentemont Abbey"). Less than a year later, he was assigned the additional duty of succeeding Franklin as Minister to France. French foreign minister [Count de Vergennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Gravier,_comte_de_Vergennes "Charles Gravier, comte de Vergennes") commented, "You replace Monsieur Franklin, I hear." Jefferson replied, "I succeed. No man can replace him."[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-122) During his five years in Paris, Jefferson played a leading role in shaping [U.S. foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._foreign_policy "U.S. foreign policy").[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-123)

In 1786, he met and fell in love with [Maria Cosway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Cosway "Maria Cosway"), a married 27-year-old musician. She returned to Great Britain after six weeks, but she and Jefferson maintained a lifelong correspondence.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-124) During the summer of 1786, Jefferson arrived in London to meet with John Adams, who was then serving as the nation's first [US Ambassador to Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Ambassador_to_Britain "US Ambassador to Britain"). Adams had official access to [George III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_III "George III") and arranged a meeting between Jefferson and the king. Jefferson later described the king's reception of the men as "ungracious". According to Adams's grandson, George III turned his back on both in a gesture of public insult. Jefferson returned to France in August.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-125)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Mather_Brown_-_Thomas_Jefferson_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Mather_Brown_-_Thomas_Jefferson_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mather_Brown_-_Thomas_Jefferson_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

1786 portrait by [Mather Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mather_Brown "Mather Brown")

Jefferson sent for his youngest surviving child, nine-year-old Polly, in June 1787. She was accompanied by 14 year old young slave from Monticello, [Sally Hemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Hemings "Sally Hemings"). Jefferson had taken her older brother, [James Hemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Hemings "James Hemings"), to Paris as part of his domestic staff and had him trained in French cuisine.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-126) According to Sally's son, [Madison Hemings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_Hemings "Madison Hemings"), by the time Sally was 16-year-old she was pregnant with 46 year old Jefferson's child.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-madisonstatement-127)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Meacham_pp._216-128) Madison indicated his mother agreed to return to the United States only after Jefferson promised to free her children when they came of age.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-madisonstatement-127)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Meacham_pp._216-128)

While in France, Jefferson became a regular companion of the [Marquis de Lafayette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquis_de_Lafayette "Marquis de Lafayette"), a [French hero of the American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_American_Revolutionary_War "France in the American Revolutionary War"), and Jefferson used his influence with Lafayette to procure trade agreements with France.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Bowers328-129)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Burstein120-130) As the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution") began, Jefferson agreed to allow his Paris residence at [Hôtel de Langeac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Langeac "Hôtel de Langeac") to be used for meetings by Lafayette and other revolutionary leaders. He was in Paris during the [storming of the Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_the_Bastille "Storming of the Bastille") on July 14, 1789, and he consulted with Lafayette as Lafayette drafted the [Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_the_Rights_of_Man_and_of_the_Citizen "Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-131) Jefferson often found his mail opened by postmasters, so he invented his own enciphering device, the "[Wheel Cipher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_disk "Jefferson disk")"; he wrote important communications in code for the rest of his career.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-132)[[k]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-133) Unable to attend the 1787 Constitution Convention, Jefferson supported the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") but desired the addition of the promised Bill of Rights.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-134) Jefferson left Paris for America in September 1789.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-135) He remained a firm supporter of the French Revolution while opposing its more violent elements.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-136)

## Secretary of State

See also: [First Party System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Party_System "First Party System") and [Relationship of Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relationship_of_Alexander_Hamilton_and_Thomas_Jefferson "Relationship of Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson")

[![Image 17: Painting of Jefferson](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Thomas_Jefferson_by_Peale_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Thomas_Jefferson_by_Peale_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Thomas_Jefferson_by_Peale_(cropped).jpg)

A 48-year-old Jefferson in 1791, in a portrait by [Charles Willson Peale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Willson_Peale "Charles Willson Peale")

Soon after returning from France, Jefferson accepted President Washington's invitation to serve as [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State").[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-137) Pressing issues at the time, the national debt and where the new national capital should be placed following its planned relocation from [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") in 1800, placed him at odds with [Secretary of the Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_the_Treasury "Secretary of the Treasury")[Alexander Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton"), who favored a capital close to major commercial centers in the [Northeast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_United_States "Northeastern United States"), while Washington, Jefferson, and other agrarians wanted it further south.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Cooke,_1970,_pp._523%E2%80%9345-138) After lengthy deadlock, the [Compromise of 1790](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compromise_of_1790 "Compromise of 1790") was struck, permanently locating the capital on the [Potomac River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potomac_River "Potomac River"), and the federal government assumed the war debts of all original [13 states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies").[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Cooke,_1970,_pp._523%E2%80%9345-138)

Jefferson opposed a national debt, preferring that each state retire its own, which contrasted with Hamilton's vision of the [federal government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") consolidating state debts[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-139) and establishing national credit and a national bank. Jefferson strenuously opposed both policies and attempted to undermine Hamilton's agenda, which nearly led Washington to dismiss him from the [cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"). He later left the cabinet voluntarily.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-140)

Jefferson's goals were to decrease American dependence on British commerce and to expand commercial trade with France. He sought to weaken [Spanish colonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas "Spanish colonization of the Americas") of the [Trans-Appalachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Appalachia "Trans-Appalachia") and British control in the North, believing this would aid in the pacification of [Native Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans "Native Americans").[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-141)

Along with political protegé [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison"), then a [U.S. Representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Representative "U.S. Representative"), and author [Philip Freneau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Freneau "Philip Freneau"), Jefferson co-founded the _[National Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Gazette "National Gazette")_ in Philadelphia in 1791, which sought to counter the policies of the [Federalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalist_Party "Federalist Party"), which Hamilton was promoting through the _[Gazette of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gazette\_of\_the\_United\_States "Gazette of the United States")_, an influential Federalist newspaper. The _National Gazette_ criticized the policies promoted by Hamilton, often in anonymous essays signed by the pen name _Brutus_ at Jefferson's urging and written by Madison.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-142) In the spring of 1791, Jefferson was suffering from [migraines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migraine "Migraine") and tiring of the infighting with Hamilton, so he and Madison departed for a vacation in [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-Randall_1996_p1-143)

In May 1792, Jefferson's concern about emerging political rivalries in the young nation was escalating, and he wrote Washington, imploring him to run for reelection for a second term [that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1792_United_States_presidential_election "1792 United States presidential election") as a unifying influence.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-144) He urged the president to rally the citizenry to a party that would defend democracy against the corrupting influence of banks and financial-focused interests, which the Federalists were embracing and espousing. Historians recognize Jefferson's letter to Washington as one of the first delineations of [Democratic-Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic-Republican_Party "Democratic-Republican Party") principles.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-145) Jefferson, Madison, and other Democratic-Republican organizers favored [states' rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States'_rights "States' rights") and local control and opposed the federal concentration of power. Hamilton, conversely, sought more power vested in the federal government.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-146)

Jefferson supported France against Britain when the two nations fought in 1793, though his arguments in Washington's Cabinet were undercut by French Revolutionary envoy [Edmond-Charles Genêt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmond-Charles_Gen%C3%AAt "Edmond-Charles Genêt")'s open scorn for Washington.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson#cite_note-147) In discussions with British Minister [George Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hammond_(diplomat) "George Hammond (diplomat)"), Jefferson tried in vain to persuade the British to vacate their posts in the Northwest and to compensate the U.S. for enslaved people freed by the British at the end of the Revolutionary War. # Early American Stances on the Size and Role of the Military and its Effects On the War of 1812

Updated July 8, 2024•July 20, 2020

[![Image 35: Google Classroom Logo](https://www.battlefields.org/themes/client/abt/static/images/icons/icon-google-classroom.png)Share to Google Classroom Added by 0 Educators](https://classroom.google.com/share?url=)
On June 18, 1812, as the United States formally declared war on Great Britain, many Americans found themselves abundantly optimistic and hopeful that Canada would quickly be captured and victory soon secured. As the former President [Thomas Jefferson](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/thomas-jefferson) remarked in a letter, “The acquisition of Canada this year … will be a mere matter of marching.” Indeed, with an overwhelming population compared to Canada and with Great Britain distracted fighting in the Napoleonic Wars, the United States seemed poised to overtake Canada by the end of the year. However, as the opening campaigns of the war illustrated, the dilapidated, decayed, and diminutive state of the United States military soon hindered such advantages. Contributing to the chaotic and unprepared condition of the United States’ military at the onset of war was the lack of unified consensus on the role and size of the military in the new republic.

![Image 36](https://www.battlefields.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_third/public/thumbnails/image/Thomas%20Jefferson%20copy.jpg.webp?itok=Ufva4IQe)

 Portrait of Thomas Jefferson by Rembrandt Peale in 1800. 

For decades prior to the outbreak of war in 1812, the United States military had seen its strength ebb and flow with the changing policies of new presidential administrations. Initially, following the election of John Adams in 1796, the fate of the national military as a valuable and formidable force seemed secured. Being a [Federalist](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/federalist-party) with the interests in a strong national government, President Adams was by nature in favor of a large and funded military. The Federalist view of the military, shared by President Adams, called for there to be a strong standing army and navy, modeled after America’s European counterparts, which could not only deter possible war but put the nation in a prepared position in case an unavoidable war was to break out. With the threat of looming war with France during his presidency, it would not take long for Adams to put these ideals into practice. Under Adams’ leadership, the peacetime army was drastically bolstered from a mere 840 men to a theoretical 10,000-man limit, although it would only swell to 5,400 under him, consisting of 12 infantry regiments, and 6 cavalry companies. In addition to the increased size of the regular army, Adams authorized the ability to summon 80,000 militiamen in case of an attack. In terms of American maritime capabilities, Adams built up the Navy to a size of 13 active frigates and 6 ships-of-the-line under construction while simultaneously pouring money into coastal defenses, as well as overseeing the re-birth of the Marine Corps. This buildup of arms served the United States invaluably in the unofficial [Quasi-War](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/quasi-war)(1798-1801) against the French, putting an end to the French harassment of American shipping in the Atlantic. Despite the success of the Federalist policies of Adams, the taxes and seemingly elitist mentality caused by a larger permanent military would pave the way for the election of Democratic-Republicans, such as Presidents Thomas Jefferson and [James Madison](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/james-madison).

While the previous administration had made great strides in preparing the nation’s defenses by investing in a strong military, after his election in 1800, Jefferson immediately began work undermining these advances of his predecessor. In stark contrast to Adams’ Federalist stance on the size of the military, Jefferson, as a staunch Democratic-Republican, fervently opposed the buildup of a national military. Democratic-Republicans, such as Jefferson, were strongly opposed to and fearful of a large federal government and an accompanying strong military, which they believed to be subversive to the democratic institutions that on which the nation was founded. In the eyes of Jefferson and his colleagues, a strong national military was inclined to become corrupt and rule tyrannically over dissenting citizens as the weapon of an overbearing central government. As Jefferson argued, "Standing armies [are] inconsistent with [a people's] freedom” and “completely adverse” to the “spirit of this country.” Instead of relying on the potentially despotic and overgrown institution of a standing military, Jefferson instead favored the use of militia. Looking to the city-states of Ancient Greece and Rome for example, Jefferson longed for an idealized agrarian society, where “every citizen” is obliged “to be a soldier” in militia service.

Shortly after taking office, Jefferson introduced sweeping reforms of the armed forces consistent with such ideals. Under the Military Peace Establishment Act, Jefferson authorized the downsizing of the army from 5,400 men to 3,300 men consisting of only two regiments of infantry, one artillery regiment, and a minuscule engineer corps. Perhaps the most dramatic consequence of these cuts was felt by the officer corps of the army. Up to one-third of the officer corps was removed, the majority being experienced and devoted Federalists, in an attempt to remove partisanship from the institution. However, these empty spots were soon filled and given as gifts to Democratic-Republican political appointees who had little interest, or knowledge, in military affairs. The consequences of such political appointments can little be understated in the effects they would have upon the War of 1812. These “imbeciles and ignoramuses,” as [Winfield Scott](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/winfield-scott) described them, would lead to such a level of incompetence and demoralization that the army would not be able to recover from until late in the War of 1812. In addition to decreasing the size of the army and reforming its officer corps, Jefferson drastically decreased the size of the navy. Believing the navy to be overly prone to drawing the nation into conflict, Jefferson cut the number of active frigates to 7 as well as halting construction on the congressionally approved ships-of-the-line. Of the first presidents of the United States, Jefferson’s tenure and anti-standing military policies would have the most lasting implications on the United States’ preparedness to go to war in 1812.

![Image 37: Portrait of President James Madison wearing a black coat and white cravat, seated before a red drapery with books visible in the background.](https://www.battlefields.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_original/public/thumbnails/image/James%20Madison_0.jpg.webp?itok=KKGcbq5T)

_James Madison_**,** 1816, by John Vanderlyn.

[Courtesy of the White House Collection](https://www.whitehousehistory.org/photos/james-madison)

Following his election in 1808, President James Madison continued Jefferson’s anti-military sentiments in his administration. Having served as Jefferson’s Secretary of State, as well as being a fellow Democratic-Republican, Madison maintained many of the inclinations of his predecessor in not wishing to expand or strengthen the military. As it had become under Jefferson’s leadership, under Madison, the military, especially the army, continued to remain neglected and festered with incompetent officers and leadership. However, as 1812 approached, with war looming on the horizon, Madison soon realized that his ideals for a small government lay in conflict with his desire for war. As Madison voiced in an address to Congress, because of Britain’s “war on our lawful commerce… Congress will feel the duty of putting the United States into an armor and an attitude demanded by the crisis.” This call for wartime preparedness by the president was embraced by Congress, leading to the most sizable increase in the strength of the military since the Quasi-war. Such legislation included measures to fill out the ranks of the army, raise more volunteers, and purchase arms for the army and navy. Understanding the pragmatism needed for the impending war, Madison had transcended his anti-military beliefs in order to bolster the armed forces.

While President Madison had made great strides in preparing the military for war, his actions were arguably too late to have an effect on the condition of the military by the outbreak of war. The army, only 7,000 strong and still plagued by incompetence in the officer corps and well-understrength, faced terrible defeats in the opening engagements of the war, while the navy, too small to have any significant effect, was confined to relatively inconsequential duels. Despite these initial setbacks, as the war would continue, young, competent officers would rise to the challenge and transform the understrength military into a well-disciplined and professional force. In addition to the ascendency of a younger, more aggressive, class of officers restoring the dignity to the military, Madison would continue in his realization of the importance of a standing military, increasing the regulation army size to 35,000 by the end of the war.

# Early American Stances on the Size and Role of the Military and its Effects On the War of 1812

Updated July 8, 2024•July 20, 2020

[![Image 35: Google Classroom Logo](https://www.battlefields.org/themes/client/abt/static/images/icons/icon-google-classroom.png)Share to Google Classroom Added by 0 Educators](https://classroom.google.com/share?url=)
On June 18, 1812, as the United States formally declared war on Great Britain, many Americans found themselves abundantly optimistic and hopeful that Canada would quickly be captured and victory soon secured. As the former President [Thomas Jefferson](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/thomas-jefferson) remarked in a letter, “The acquisition of Canada this year … will be a mere matter of marching.” Indeed, with an overwhelming population compared to Canada and with Great Britain distracted fighting in the Napoleonic Wars, the United States seemed poised to overtake Canada by the end of the year. However, as the opening campaigns of the war illustrated, the dilapidated, decayed, and diminutive state of the United States military soon hindered such advantages. Contributing to the chaotic and unprepared condition of the United States’ military at the onset of war was the lack of unified consensus on the role and size of the military in the new republic.

![Image 36](https://www.battlefields.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_third/public/thumbnails/image/Thomas%20Jefferson%20copy.jpg.webp?itok=Ufva4IQe)

 Portrait of Thomas Jefferson by Rembrandt Peale in 1800. 

For decades prior to the outbreak of war in 1812, the United States military had seen its strength ebb and flow with the changing policies of new presidential administrations. Initially, following the election of John Adams in 1796, the fate of the national military as a valuable and formidable force seemed secured. Being a [Federalist](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/federalist-party) with the interests in a strong national government, President Adams was by nature in favor of a large and funded military. The Federalist view of the military, shared by President Adams, called for there to be a strong standing army and navy, modeled after America’s European counterparts, which could not only deter possible war but put the nation in a prepared position in case an unavoidable war was to break out. With the threat of looming war with France during his presidency, it would not take long for Adams to put these ideals into practice. Under Adams’ leadership, the peacetime army was drastically bolstered from a mere 840 men to a theoretical 10,000-man limit, although it would only swell to 5,400 under him, consisting of 12 infantry regiments, and 6 cavalry companies. In addition to the increased size of the regular army, Adams authorized the ability to summon 80,000 militiamen in case of an attack. In terms of American maritime capabilities, Adams built up the Navy to a size of 13 active frigates and 6 ships-of-the-line under construction while simultaneously pouring money into coastal defenses, as well as overseeing the re-birth of the Marine Corps. This buildup of arms served the United States invaluably in the unofficial [Quasi-War](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/articles/quasi-war)(1798-1801) against the French, putting an end to the French harassment of American shipping in the Atlantic. Despite the success of the Federalist policies of Adams, the taxes and seemingly elitist mentality caused by a larger permanent military would pave the way for the election of Democratic-Republicans, such as Presidents Thomas Jefferson and [James Madison](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/james-madison).

While the previous administration had made great strides in preparing the nation’s defenses by investing in a strong military, after his election in 1800, Jefferson immediately began work undermining these advances of his predecessor. In stark contrast to Adams’ Federalist stance on the size of the military, Jefferson, as a staunch Democratic-Republican, fervently opposed the buildup of a national military. Democratic-Republicans, such as Jefferson, were strongly opposed to and fearful of a large federal government and an accompanying strong military, which they believed to be subversive to the democratic institutions that on which the nation was founded. In the eyes of Jefferson and his colleagues, a strong national military was inclined to become corrupt and rule tyrannically over dissenting citizens as the weapon of an overbearing central government. As Jefferson argued, "Standing armies [are] inconsistent with [a people's] freedom” and “completely adverse” to the “spirit of this country.” Instead of relying on the potentially despotic and overgrown institution of a standing military, Jefferson instead favored the use of militia. Looking to the city-states of Ancient Greece and Rome for example, Jefferson longed for an idealized agrarian society, where “every citizen” is obliged “to be a soldier” in militia service.

Shortly after taking office, Jefferson introduced sweeping reforms of the armed forces consistent with such ideals. Under the Military Peace Establishment Act, Jefferson authorized the downsizing of the army from 5,400 men to 3,300 men consisting of only two regiments of infantry, one artillery regiment, and a minuscule engineer corps. Perhaps the most dramatic consequence of these cuts was felt by the officer corps of the army. Up to one-third of the officer corps was removed, the majority being experienced and devoted Federalists, in an attempt to remove partisanship from the institution. However, these empty spots were soon filled and given as gifts to Democratic-Republican political appointees who had little interest, or knowledge, in military affairs. The consequences of such political appointments can little be understated in the effects they would have upon the War of 1812. These “imbeciles and ignoramuses,” as [Winfield Scott](https://www.battlefields.org/learn/biographies/winfield-scott) described them, would lead to such a level of incompetence and demoralization that the army would not be able to recover from until late in the War of 1812. In addition to decreasing the size of the army and reforming its officer corps, Jefferson drastically decreased the size of the navy. Believing the navy to be overly prone to drawing the nation into conflict, Jefferson cut the number of active frigates to 7 as well as halting construction on the congressionally approved ships-of-the-line. Of the first presidents of the United States, Jefferson’s tenure and anti-standing military policies would have the most lasting implications on the United States’ preparedness to go to war in 1812.

![Image 37: Portrait of President James Madison wearing a black coat and white cravat, seated before a red drapery with books visible in the background.](https://www.battlefields.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_original/public/thumbnails/image/James%20Madison_0.jpg.webp?itok=KKGcbq5T)

_James Madison_**,** 1816, by John Vanderlyn.

[Courtesy of the White House Collection](https://www.whitehousehistory.org/photos/james-madison)

Following his election in 1808, President James Madison continued Jefferson’s anti-military sentiments in his administration. Having served as Jefferson’s Secretary of State, as well as being a fellow Democratic-Republican, Madison maintained many of the inclinations of his predecessor in not wishing to expand or strengthen the military. As it had become under Jefferson’s leadership, under Madison, the military, especially the army, continued to remain neglected and festered with incompetent officers and leadership. However, as 1812 approached, with war looming on the horizon, Madison soon realized that his ideals for a small government lay in conflict with his desire for war. As Madison voiced in an address to Congress, because of Britain’s “war on our lawful commerce… Congress will feel the duty of putting the United States into an armor and an attitude demanded by the crisis.” This call for wartime preparedness by the president was embraced by Congress, leading to the most sizable increase in the strength of the military since the Quasi-war. Such legislation included measures to fill out the ranks of the army, raise more volunteers, and purchase arms for the army and navy. Understanding the pragmatism needed for the impending war, Madison had transcended his anti-military beliefs in order to bolster the armed forces.

While President Madison had made great strides in preparing the military for war, his actions were arguably too late to have an effect on the condition of the military by the outbreak of war. The army, only 7,000 strong and still plagued by incompetence in the officer corps and well-understrength, faced terrible defeats in the opening engagements of the war, while the navy, too small to have any significant effect, was confined to relatively inconsequential duels. Despite these initial setbacks, as the war would continue, young, competent officers would rise to the challenge and transform the understrength military into a well-disciplined and professional force. In addition to the ascendency of a younger, more aggressive, class of officers restoring the dignity to the military, Madison would continue in his realization of the importance of a standing military, increasing the regulation army size to 35,000 by the end of the war.
